lede: Sometimes the unknown is the power itself. You cannot divide a power away, so the equation looks stuck. Taking logarithms of both sides brings the index down to the front, and what is left is an ordinary linear equation you already know how to solve.
can: Take logarithms of both sides and bring the index down with brackets
Expand, collect the x terms on one side and factorise to reach x
Keep full accuracy until the last step and answer to the accuracy asked for

text: When the unknown has climbed into the power

md:
$2^{x} = 40$ looks like nothing you can rearrange. Dividing by $2$ does not touch the $x$, because the $x$ is an index rather than a multiplier.
A logarithm is the tool that moves it. Take logs of both sides and the power law turns $\log 2^{x}$ into $x \log 2$, so the $x$ becomes an ordinary factor and the equation becomes linear.

prompt: One tap to begin. In the picture above, $2^{x} = 40$ becomes $x \log 2 = \log 40$. Which law of logarithms did that?
explain: $\log a^{n} = n \log a$ is the power law. It is the only one that moves an index, and it is the first line of every question of this kind.

md:
Solve $5^{3x - 2} = 40$.
**Step 1.** Take logs of both sides.
**Step 2.** The power law brings the whole index down, in brackets: $(3x - 2) \log 5 = \log 40$.
**Step 3.** Divide by $\log 5$, then tidy the linear equation.
**Step 4.** Evaluate once, at the end: $x = 1.43$ to two decimal places.

title: Why taking logs frees the unknown
md: Every $\log$ in these lines is just a number, so once the index is down at the front the equation is linear in $x$ and the ordinary rules apply. That is the whole purpose of the first line: it changes what kind of equation you are looking at.

prompt: Working on $5^{3x - 2} = 40$: taking logs and dividing gives $3x - 2 = \frac{\log 40}{\log 5}$. What is $x$, correct to two decimal places?

md:
The index is a whole expression, so all of it comes down together and all of it needs a bracket: $(4x + 1) \log 2$, never $4x + 1 \log 2$.
Without the bracket the logarithm multiplies only the last term, and the equation being solved is no longer the one that was set. It is the single most reported slip on this topic.

title: Summer 2018, Unit 1, Question 6
md: Most candidates knew to take logarithms and the question was answered well. The marks that went were careless: the brackets left off the index, and bases other than ten producing extra slips. Isolating the unknown was the hurdle for everyone else.

prompt: Taking logs of $2^{4x + 1} = 7^{x + 3}$ gives which line?
explain: Each whole index comes down in front of its own logarithm, inside a bracket. Without the brackets the logarithms multiply only the constants.

md:
With logarithms on both sides there are two $x$ terms. Expand each bracket, move the $x$ terms to one side and the numbers to the other, then factorise $x$ out.
Every $\log$ here is just a number, so treat them exactly as you would treat any letters in a linear equation. The sign is what goes wrong: a term that crosses the equals sign changes sign.

prompt: From the working shown above, $x(4 \log 2 - \log 7) = 3 \log 7 - \log 2$. What is $x$, correct to two decimal places?
explain: The bracket on the left is $0.359022$ and the right-hand side is $2.234264$, so $x = 6.22$.

md:
Keep the logarithms as logarithms all the way down the page and let the calculator do the whole expression in one step. Rounding $\log 11$ and $\log 3$ on the way changes the answer in the second decimal place, which is exactly where the mark is.
Unless a question says otherwise, give two decimal places.

title: Solving Index Equations using Logs - Part 1 - Corbettmaths
why: The same four moves worked through on several equations, with the brackets written every time.

prompt: Solve $3^{x} = 11$, giving your answer correct to two decimal places. Keep the logarithms in the calculator until the final step.
explain: $x = \frac{\log 11}{\log 3} = 2.182658$, which is $2.18$. Rounding each logarithm first would give $2.17$.

md:
Recognise that an unknown in the index needs logarithms, not division.
Take logs of both sides and bring each whole index down inside a bracket.
Expand, collect the $x$ terms on one side and factorise $x$ out.
Divide and evaluate in one calculator step at the end.
Spot when both sides share a base, and solve by equating indices instead.

This is a standard $4$ or $5$ mark part, usually the second half of a logarithm question. The first mark is taking logs of both sides; the last is the answer to two decimal places. Stuck? Write the logs of both sides and bring each index down in a bracket — that line alone earns the first two marks, whatever happens afterwards.
